title: Relational algebra
lead: From declarative SQL to relational operators, set semantics and composed query plans.

sections.title: Query languages and relational algebra
sections.html:
SQL describes a required result; relational algebra describes transformations of relations. A DBMS translates the query into a logical plan, applies equivalence-preserving rewrites and selects physical operators. Codd’s theorem connects relational algebra with the domain-independent relational calculus.

Each relational-algebra operator takes relation instances and returns a relation instance. This closure property allows operators to be composed into a query tree. Input schemas determine output schemas and allow invalid expressions to be rejected before execution.

Pure relational algebra uses sets, so a relation contains no duplicate tuples. SQL uses bags by default. When moving between them, duplicate elimination must be accounted for explicitly.

PDF pp. 1–7

sections.title: Selection and projection
sections.html:
Selection σp(R) keeps exactly the tuples of R satisfying predicate p. It changes the rows but keeps the input schema. Predicates can combine conditions with conjunction and disjunction.

Projection πA(R) keeps the attributes listed in A. Its output schema is that attribute list. Under set semantics, tuples that become identical after projection collapse into one tuple. SQL SELECT without DISTINCT normally retains their multiplicities.

Selection and projection therefore operate on different dimensions of a relation: selection restricts tuples, while projection restricts attributes. Their position in a composed expression determines which attributes must remain available to later operators.

PDF pp. 8–9

sections.title: Union, difference, product and renaming
sections.html:
Union R ∪ S and difference R − S require compatible schemas: the same number of attributes and compatible types at corresponding positions. Union contains tuples in either input; difference contains tuples in R that are absent from S. Difference is not commutative. Intersection can be expressed as R − (R − S).

The Cartesian product R × S pairs every tuple of R with every tuple of S, yielding |R|·|S| tuples. The output contains attributes from both relations. Renaming ρ supplies relation or attribute names where names would otherwise collide.

SQL UNION, EXCEPT and INTERSECT use duplicate elimination. Their ALL variants use bag multiplicities: union adds counts, intersection takes their minimum, and difference takes max(mR − mS, 0). SQLite does not implement EXCEPT ALL or INTERSECT ALL.

PDF pp. 10–14

sections.title: Joins and additional operators
sections.html:
A theta join is R ⋈θ S = σθ(R × S). An equijoin uses equality predicates. A natural join equates every shared attribute name and projects away the duplicate copies of those attributes. A self-join uses two renamed references to the same relation.

The product-and-selection definition specifies the result, not a requirement to materialise the product. Physical join algorithms compute the same result more efficiently.

Extended algebra includes grouping and aggregation γ, duplicate elimination δ, sorting τ, assignment and division. A logical plan specifies these relational operations; a physical plan additionally selects implementations such as an index scan or sort-merge join.

PDF pp. 15–20

quiz.question: If R has 3 rows and S has 4 rows, how many rows does R × S contain?
quiz.explanation: Each R row combines with every S row: 3×4=12. The Cartesian product has not yet applied a join condition; a later selection may reduce the number of pairs.
